https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c304.text: Image source, NSW Police Image caption, Lily Hooper, 18, was found dead after an eight-day search in the Australian bush By Tabby Wilson Published 20 August 2026, 04:16 BST Updated 52 minutes ago The body of a woman has been found in Australian bushland, following an eight-day search for a Sydney teenager reported missing last Wednesday. Police said that while the body was yet to be formally identified, it was believed to be that of 18-year-old Lily Hooper. The confirmation came after the state premier told the New South Wales parliament that she had been found alive before later retracting the statement. The teenager left her home in Sydney to go walking in a nearby national park on 12 August. Her family reported her missing later that night, after she failed to return home by 10pm. Her car was found in a car park at the bottom of a challenging trail in the Nattai National Park. Police said that the body was found in the Southern Highlands at approximately 11:30 local time on Thursday. Hooper's body had been found in dense vegetation and would likely have to be carried out on foot. There was initial confusion as to Hooper's condition, after New South Wales Premier Chris Minns told a parliamentary hearing that she had been found alive. Local media suggested that her family had also been informed that she was alive. Minns corrected himself shortly afterwards, and told the hearing that "Lily's body has been found" and she was deceased. "This is obviously devastating, and I'm profoundly sad for her family and for all those concerned," said Minns, and apologised to the committee. In a press conference on Thursday afternoon, Assistant Police Commissioner Joseph Cassar did not directly respond to questions as to how Hooper's family came to be told she had been found alive. He told reporters that there was a period of between eight to 10 minutes before the teenager's parents were given an updated report on her condition. He said he did not know exactly what was said to the Hooper family, but that if he "could turn the clock back, I would certainly". A multi-agency search for the missing bushwalker had taken place over the past week, with support from multiple NSW Police Force units including PolAir, the Rescue Unit, the Trail Bike Unit, the Mounted Unit and the Dog Unit. Police have also been supported by the Rural Fire Service, the National Parks and Wildlife Service and almost 100 members of the Australian Defence Force. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese paid tribute to the 18-year-old in parliament, calling Hooper's death an unspeakable tragedy. "Lily Hooper had so much more to offer the world. Her passing, I have no doubt, will be felt very deeply," he said. Opposition leader Angus Taylor, Hooper's local MP, said the initial incorrect reports that Hooper had been found alive made the family's loss even worse. "We can only imagine what Lily's family is going through right now. Such news would be a nightmare for any parent, and we grieve for Lily's wider family," Taylor said. https://www.politico.eu/article/le-pen-s.text: A U.S. plan to ban diesel exports would have "incalculable" consequences for French people, warned Marine Le Pen, the far-right candidate in the French presidential elections, at the POLITICO Playbook Paris Live event Thursday. The surge in fuel prices “hits all French people really hard” and is “their main concern” right now, Le Pen added. The Trump Administration is floating a potential ban on exports of diesel for 90 days in a bid to bring down energy prices, POLITICO reported on Wednesday. While the European Commission says it is pressuring the White House to drop the idea, some European authorities have downplayed the threats despite warnings it could have devastating consequences on the bloc's fuel supply. Advertisement Advertisement The EU currently imports more than half of its diesel from America and imports have increased in recent months to make up for those lost due to the conflict in the Middle East. Prices and supply have been further affected by strikes on Russian oil refineries. Le Pen said the government should adopt her proposal to cut VAT on fuel as prices at the pump surge across the country and stoke fears of a new Yellow Jackets-style protest movement. “The role of a political leader is precisely to ensure that the French people do not have to take to the streets to secure a decision that is both long-awaited and absolutely necessary,” she said, noting that other European countries like Spain and Germany had similarly decided to cut taxes on fuel given how the conflict in the Middle East has led to worldwide oil price spikes.

http://www.liherald.com/stories/peter-ki.text: Log in Monday, September 28, 2026 Complete forecast Peter King: The United States needs to be a dependable ally Whether it’s the war in Iran, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, China’s expansionism or the continuing threat of Islamist terrorism, the United States and the world are faced with crises from multiple directions. This should be a time when nations with common values and interests forge a united front, no matter our policy differences or personality clashes. The most significant example of this unity occurred at the close of World War II, when the U.S., Canada and the countries of Western Europe put aside historic differences and rivalries to unite against the common threat of world communism emanating from the Soviet Union by forming NATO, which became the largest and most successful military and governmental alliance in human history. After centuries of conflict, including World Wars I and II, which resulted in the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Americans, NATO ultimately caused the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, and prevented the invasion of one country by another on the continent of Europe for 75 years, until Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. As the world’s lone superpower, the U.S. was the main force within NATO, providing troops on the ground in various countries, a nuclear umbrella for all of the organization’s members and, most important, our credibility and commitment. The member countries were of course also essential to NATO’s success, coordinating their military units under an American Supreme Command and pledging unity. No wonder it has been Russian President Vladimir Putin’s long-held dream to somehow bring about NATO’s dissolution. NATO demonstrated its commitment to stand united when it responded so quickly and forcefully to the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001. Though no other NATO country was attacked and there was no war on European soil, countries responded with troops, courage and ability. Great Britain, Denmark, Canada, Poland and Italy would suffer casualties at a per-capita rate which approached our own. Previously, in the successful Operation Desert Storm against Iraq in 1991, countries such as Britain and France sent troops to fight alongside American forces. NATO did, however, develop lingering deficiencies. Its over-reliance on the United States led to a continuing failure by member countries to meet their financial commitments to the alliance. I recall being at a meeting in London with Britain’s defense minister as far back as 1997, where he acknowledged the fear of NATO’s becoming a “paper tiger.” It is to Present Trump’s credit that he effectively saved the alliance by pressuring its member nations to pay up. Trump’s more recent actions, however — his threats to take Greenland from Denmark, engaging in a tariff war with Canada while referring to it as our 51st state, his exchange of insults with Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, and his attack on Pope Leo— have only weakened NATO. Similarly, Trump’s withdrawal of troops from Poland and Germany, and cuts in aid to Ukraine, have raised doubts about American credibility and reliability. Also damaging to the alliance was the failure to coordinate strategy with NATO countries before beginning the war against Iran. (This was so contrary to the close cooperation I saw between American and British generals when I had visited Afghanistan.) This has resulted in Britain’s refusal to provide its minesweeping capability to Trump in the Strait of Hormuz, and Meloni’s denying us use of air bases in Italy. These actions, on both sides, are shortsighted, and counterproductive to everyone. There is no doubt that the United States is the superpower and indispensable partner in the alliance. It is also true that our relationship with NATO, and our actions and level of support for Ukraine, South Korea, Taiwan and Israel, are watched carefully by our adversaries China, Iran, North Korea, Al Qaeda and ISIS, as well as by our allies and friendly nations such as Japan and the Philippines in the Pacific and Egypt, Jordan and the United Arab Emirates in the Middle East. As strong as the U.S. is, maintaining alliances and international support is vital to our national security. Isolationist policies such as America First and Fortress America have failed us in the past, and we can’t afford to rely on, or even experiment with them again. We live in an ever more dangerous, threatening world. We cannot risk America First becoming America Alone. Peter King is a former congressman, and a former chair of the House Committee on Homeland Security. Comments? pking@ liherald.com. Please join us here . At least 10 people were killed in a train crash in central Spain on Wednesday morning, local authorities have confirmed. "The information we are receiving is not good at all," a spokeswoman for the government of the Castilla-La Mancha region told local media, giving an initial death toll of ten. "There has been a collision between two trains [and] there are injured people," added Manuel Galans, mayor of the town of Urda in the province of Toledo, near to where the incident took place just after 9 a.m. local time. The mayor of another nearby village, Jesus Perez of Los Yebenes, told Spanish TV that the accident appeared "serious." Spanish Health Minister Monica Garcia told local broadcaster TVE that it was a "high impact accident, it will be a major tragedy" but said it was too soon to confirm a final casualty figure. "We don't just need help from nearby hospitals, we need nearby hospitals that have ICU beds," she added. Spain train crash: what do we know? The cause of the collision was not immediately known, but initial reports suggested one train had slammed into the back of another train which had been stationary. "We heard a massive roar, a truly ​enormous thud ‌that went on for 10 seconds as if the train were about to derail," one passenger, Miguel, told local radio station COPE. "Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train – I imagine it must have been the other one." Images from the scene showed at least two severely damaged train carriages flipped over on their side after tumbling down an embankment. Ten people have been killed in a train crash in Spain which has seen several such accidents in recent years Image: Juanma Jiménez/EUROPA PRESS/dpa/picture alliance One of the trains, operated by AVE, was reportedly carrying 397 passengers while the other, operated by IRYO, had 146 people on board, according to the Castilla-La Mancha local government spokeswoman. A reporter for local broadcaster TVE described scenes of "absolute chaos" and a constant stream of ambulances and emergency vehicles. El Pais cited witnesses describing numerous injuries and ​arrival of emergency medical teams at the scene. "All resources are currently being deployed," spokesperson for the Spanish emergency services told the AFP news agency, including "several fire crews, three helicopters, and two mobile intensive care units." In a post on social media, rail operator Adif confirmed that "traffic ​on the Madrid-Andalusia high-speed rail line ​has been suspended following a rear-end collision ​between two trains." Spanish PM Sanchez 'shocked' by 'serious' accident Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said he was "shocked" by the "serious" accident. "Emergency services are working on the ground to assist those affected and ensure their safety, in coordination with all the involved administrations," he wrote on social media. "My affection, solidarity and support to all the victims and their families." The collision comes just months after another devastating rail disaster near Adamuz in Andalusia in January . In that accident, a high-speed train derailed and collided with an oncoming train, killing 46 people and injuring more than 150. The crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people. The January incident shook the confidence the European country has in its extensive high-speed rail network.
